title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 16: Maximum Benefits for All Judicial Employees
keywords: Maximum Benefits for All Judicial Employees
Special Allowance for Justices and Judges
safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity
primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- the address CJP gave on June 21, 2006, his sixth month in office, to the heads of Supreme Court offices and the leaders of judiciary employee organizations, explaining his policy of granting employees the maximum benefits allowed by law and how it had been carried out.

A technical account of the four legal routes by which a Chief Justice can grant benefits: the sole exclusive power over 80 percent of the Judiciary Development Fund under PD 1949, realignment of the judiciary budget under the Appropriations Law and CFAG resolutions, additional allowances from surplus SAJ collections under RA 9227, and the regular benefits carried in the General Appropriations Act.

The accounting of what was actually released in the first half of 2006 -- monthly JDF disbursements totaling P17,600, roughly P57,000 per employee since December 21, 2005, a three-tier scheme favoring the lowest-paid, higher SC Praise awards, retirement cash awards and service awards -- plus planned welfare programs in housing, health and laptop acquisition.

The two reasons he gives for the policy -- compassion rooted in his own poverty as a boy and fairness owed by a government that demands total loyalty -- and the return he asks for: dedication, honesty and loyalty, the DHL norms.
sub_topics: The occasion: his 6th month in office, celebrated with the heads of offices and the leaders of the judiciary's employee organizations, as a chance to expound on his benefits policy.

The backstory of the policy announcement: he took his oath as the 21st Chief Justice on December 21, 2005, a Wednesday, and the Yuletide holidays meant his first address to the rank and file came at the flag ceremony of Monday, January 2, 2006.

That morning he stood at attention through the National Anthem, the Supreme Court and Judiciary Hymns and the Pledge of Allegiance while still in pain from surgery three days earlier, hid his affliction, and announced his maximum-benefits policy.
First route -- PD 1949, giving the Chief Justice the 'sole exclusive power' to distribute 80 percent of the Judiciary Development Fund to augment the allowances of members and personnel.

Second route -- realignment of the judiciary budget under the Appropriations Law and Joint Resolution Nos. 1 and 90 of the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group, transferring savings to augment items, though augmentation may go to items other than personnel benefits.

Third route -- RA 9227, allowing additional allowances from surplus collections of the Special Allowance for Justices and Judges, which doubled judicial compensation by 25 percent a year for four years from November 2003 to a 100 percent increase in November 2006, funded from increased docket and legal fees.

Fourth route -- the Supreme Court's regular budget under the General Appropriations Act, carrying performance and productivity incentive bonuses, clothing allowance and additional compensation (Adcom) granted uniformly across government.
The month-by-month JDF releases of the first half of 2006: P2,500 each in January, February and March, P3,800 in April, P2,900 in May and P3,400 in June -- a total of P17,600.
The policy of regularity: because JDF-funded COLA fluctuated with actual collections from the field, he set a floor of at least P2,500 monthly, disbursed in the first week of each month.

The three-tier classification recommended by the Fiscal Management and Budget Office, following the JDF Law's policy of giving the highest share to the lowest-ranked: those earning P7,000 or less, those above P7,000 up to P10,000, and those above P10,000, with the first group receiving the highest JDF COLA.

The result claimed: about P57,000 released to each member of the personnel between December 21, 2005 and June 21, 2006, effectively doubling many basic monthly salaries -- his stated goal of matching for the rank and file what RA 9227 did for justices and judges.

The incentive awards: on the recommendation of the SC Praise Committee, the model-employee award raised from P15,000 to P20,000, the award for the five finalists in the Search for Model Employees from P1,000 to P5,000, and a special P5,000 award for perfect attendance in 2005 on the chronolog time recorder.

Retirement recognition: branded wristwatches and certificates of appreciation for 10 compulsory retirees at the June 19 flag-raising, on top of the P20,000 cash award he authorized on January 31, 2006 for each retiree about a week before retirement.

Welfare programs still to come: a judiciary housing project, a more comprehensive health and medical plan, and a separate fund letting rank-and-file employees acquire laptop computers like those available to judges and court attorneys.
Reason one, compassion: having been very poor himself, he identifies with the employees' struggles and hopes that better pay will make them less vulnerable to the temptations of corruption.
Reason two, fairness: a government that demands total loyalty and all-out performance must, whenever legally and financially possible, compensate its workers properly.

What he asks in exchange -- dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and loyalty to the Supreme Court and the judiciary -- with written feedback requested from the employee-organization leaders within a month on how the DHL norms have been implemented.

stances.claim: The Chief Justice should grant judiciary employees the maximum benefits allowed by law and within his discretion, and this policy was in fact carried out in his first six months.
stances.rhetorical_move: policy stated then audited: naming the four legal sources of authority, then tabling the month-by-month releases and per-employee totals as proof of performance

stances.claim: Granting maximum benefits is first a matter of compassion, because someone who has been very poor understands the longings and frustrations of the impoverished.
stances.rhetorical_move: autobiographical warrant: hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes offered as the ground of his identification with the rank and file

stances.claim: Better compensation is, more importantly, a matter of fairness: a government that demands total loyalty and all-out performance must compensate its workers properly whenever legally and financially possible.
stances.rhetorical_move: escalation from sentiment to obligation -- compassion first, then the stronger reciprocity argument that reframes benefits as a debt rather than a gift

stances.claim: Adequate pay makes employees less vulnerable to the temptations of corruption, so the benefits policy serves the anti-corruption agenda as well as the employees.
stances.rhetorical_move: linking welfare to integrity: benefits justified instrumentally as a defense against one of the ACID problems, with DHL norms demanded in return

notable_anecdotes: On January 2, 2006, three days after surgery on December 30, 2005, he stood at attention through the National Anthem, the Supreme Court and Judiciary Hymns and the Pledge of Allegiance while profusely perspiring from surgical pain, hid his affliction, never mentioned the operation, and announced his maximum-benefits policy from the microphone.

He recalls his own childhood poverty -- hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes on the streets of Manila, and selling textbooks to classmates and Bibles to his professors and school officials to get through his education.

He describes the June 19 flag-raising at which branded wristwatches and certificates of appreciation were handed to 10 compulsory retirees, on top of the P20,000 cash award he had authorized each of them in January.
He mentions the special P5,000 award granted to an employee who registered perfect attendance for the whole of 2005 on the chronolog time recorder machine.
He tells the employee leaders he is asking for written feedback within a month on how they have concretely implemented the DHL norms -- dedication, honesty and loyalty.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' reproduces the address Chief Justice Panganiban delivered on June 21, 2006, his sixth month in office, to the heads of Supreme Court offices and the leaders of the judiciary's employee organizations. He recalled taking his oath as the 21st Chief Justice on December 21, 2005, and delivering his first address to the rank and file at the flag ceremony of January 2, 2006, when, still in pain from surgery three days earlier and profusely perspiring, he hid his affliction and announced his policy of giving employees the maximum benefits allowed by law and within his discretion. He then set out the four ways a Chief Justice can grant benefits: the 'sole exclusive power' under PD 1949 to distribute 80 percent of the Judiciary Development Fund; realignment of the judiciary budget under the Appropriations Law and CFAG Joint Resolutions 1 and 90; additional allowances from surplus collections of the Special Allowance for Justices and Judges under RA 9227, which doubled judicial pay in four annual 25 percent increments from November 2003; and the regular benefits carried in the General Appropriations Act. He accounted for the first half of 2006 month by month -- P2,500 each in January, February and March, P3,800 in April, P2,900 in May and P3,400 in June, totaling P17,600 -- explained that he had set a P2,500 monthly floor because JDF collections fluctuated, and described the three-tier classification recommended by the Fiscal Management and Budget Office that gave the largest shares to those earning P7,000 or less. He estimated that about P57,000 had been released to each employee since December, effectively doubling many basic salaries, and listed increased SC Praise awards, a perfect-attendance award, retirement cash awards and service wristwatches, plus planned housing, health and laptop-acquisition programs. He gave two reasons: compassion, having been very poor himself, hawking newspapers, shining shoes and peddling cigarettes as a boy; and, more importantly, fairness, since a government demanding total loyalty must compensate properly. In exchange he asked for dedication, honesty and loyalty -- the DHL norms -- and written feedback within a month.
